279.s: Hug says one must love the music and is proud of his reputation; the interview closes.
279.q: Well, I think, Charlie, that first of all, you really have to like what you're doing, which is most important. And I have liked music, I've liked jazz music all my life, been around many, many greats, and I feel quite flattered to be associated with these people. And I'm really, really proud of the…

846.t: Concluding views on acceptance of jazz in New Orleans
846.s: He sees growing acceptance through church talks and Tulane's interest, and the interviewer closes the session.
846.q: Well, I would say this in conclusion, that, uh, I'm very happy to see, uh, Oh, incidentally, several of the other places where I spoke was very interesting to me. It's been in different church denominations, Jewish, Methodist, Episcopal. In the churches? In the churches, in the rectories. Before…

295.t: Closing words and the Dennechine fire company
295.s: Allen invites closing words; Jack describes organizing a fire company with his wife's help and the recent Tulane Avenue parade of old volunteers.
295.ch: Mrs. Laine and the fire company
295.q: Speaking about the fire company, I organized a Dennechine fire company about 15 years ago. And through the help and the assistance of my good wife, we made it a success. It's still progressing today, and we're doing remarkably well. Now, as I said before, we were on that parade up there on Tulane…

967.t: Let's Make a Better World and closing thanks
967.s: King plays Let's Make a Better World and the host thanks everyone.
967.ch: Songwriting and the future of New Orleans music
967.q: Why don't we, I think we'll have to end it, why don't we end it, you're doing a song, and maybe it's apropos of, Let's Make a Better World. Yeah. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. The world we know, build on skills, that world's gone, don't kill. Out the sweat, tired of mine, wouldn't be…

25.s: The interviewer winds up and Taylor thanks him.
25.q: Well, the only thing that I would like to add, that I'm proud of you. Thank you.

674.t: Final thoughts on mentors, community and goodbyes
674.s: Baron shares his view of making things right, the older mentors and a joke about a concert, then they thank each other.
674.q: I’m also trying to figure it out. Like I say, there’s a certain current, the way things are going on in the world, you don’t stand on a hill and say, “Wait a minute you’re all wrong.” There’s a momentum from the last twenty or thirty years going a certain way. You just try to do what you can…

987.s: Closing compliments, Brecker's humility, and thanks for the archive videos.
987.q: But that’s what’s part of it. You know I still feel like I’m starting out. I still feel like I’m trying to learn the trumpet. You know I’m just like everyone else, believe me.

132.s: Fillius expresses gratitude, Rowe says no one has been more interesting, and they sign off.
132.q: No, it’s been a wonderful experience, a wonderful opportunity to be able to do this. And I’m everlastingly grateful to you and to the powers that be at this college to make it happen, because I don’t think it would have happened otherwise. And we did something that really needs to be done. And if…

792.s: Thanks, a hope for Part Two, and Chubby's tribute to his wife.
792.q: I’d love it. I’m very grateful and thankful for the opportunity to say things, because you know age is starting to pile up, and if I have an opportunity every now and then to be something which was Chubby. You know, it’s a groove for me too, man.

530.s: Rowe thanks Jordan for his wisdom, who invites more questions.
530.ch: New Orleans families, lifestyle and retirement
530.q: You can ask me whatever you want to ask me now, ‘cause, you’ll say oh man I should have asked him this and I didn’t. I know how it is.

337.t: Mean to Me recording, new piano duo album and goodbye
337.s: He talks about the record at his daughter's wedding, his new piano-and-sax album, and says goodbye.
337.q: See and I don’t put it on at the house, but I hear it at other places. My daughter played it at her wedding for dinner music too.

842.s: Mead calls it a remarkable time and hopes to play to 95; Rowe praises the band and thanks him.
842.q: No, I think we’ve covered it. It was a remarkable time in my life. I think back to those days with just the greatest happiness. And I’m loving playing with the Alumni All-Stars now, so music is just a happy thread and I just hope I can keep playing ‘till I’m 95 like my dad did.

349.s: Mullins hopes for more publicity for jazz; thanks and goodbye.
349.q: Well I hope that you remember all I said to you, because I think that’s probably one of our — we don’t get enough publicity. A lot of people don’t even know about us. And I’m hoping every year, I’m hoping that the tide will turn.

464.t: Closing thoughts on loving being a musician and thanks
464.s: He says he still practices and plays worldwide, feels lucky to be paid for what he loves, and the two thank each other.

141.t: Thanks and end of the interview
141.s: Panken thanks the three and the transcript ends.
141.q: Thank you. Well, I haven’t been very...

503.q: Okay. Brown:…of our trying to have your life in music, your thoughts, your philosophies and your passion…

101.q: Thank you so much. If you need anything else added from time to time, just call me up and come on back and we’ll do some more.

144.t: Closing thanks and hopes for the project
144.s: Fuller thanks the Smithsonian for preserving artists' stories, hopes it will help listeners and says it may be the last his family hears of him.
144.q: I would like to say this on behalf of you gentlemen I thank you for taking your time out from your very interesting work that you do, that you’ve done, and that you will be doing in the future with different artists like myself, or with different jazz masters. We are just regular guys. I appreciate…

62.s: Wilson says he is very religious, recalls his mother playing in church, and ends the interview with thanks.
62.q: It’ll happen, yes, I’m very religious, very religious. My mother played in the church, she played in the school, I was in church everyday when I was a kid. I stopped going after I left home [laughs] and I don’t go to church, you know, I haven’t been to church in a long time, but I respect it to the…

123.t: Closing thanks and a street naming
123.s: Kimery thanks Segal, mentions a street naming, and ends the session.
123.q: Yeah they’ve been so busy with their hitting on each other about the new election coming up for governor and all that, they haven’t paid attention to this, you know. Cause we’re just small fry.

377.s: Kuehl ends the interview; Basie thanks God and people.
377.q: I'm very happy (inaudible) people. [to play for] [Thank God and people.]

89.s: Montgomery thanks Bushell and the recording ends.
89.q: Garvin, I'd like to just and a little to what you're saying now, and express myself and mention one thing in particular. What a pleasure it's been forme just to meet and to know you. You've been a great inspiration for me and I've got a strong feeling you will be for the whole community with an…

167.s: Rosenberg asks if Bunn wants to add anything, and Bunn praises him.
167.q: No, but I still think you are a wonderful person and I'm doing all I can to help you.

234.t: Project credits: National Endowment for the Arts and Jazz Interactions
234.s: Johnston credits the NEA, Jazz Interactions and Pastor John Gensel.
234.q: Endowment for the Arts in Washington. As a matter of fact, it is one of their projects and has been administered by the Jazz Interaction in New York for which Lois McCloud is the project coordinator.

125.s: Dance praises his unchanged standards; Thompson thanks Helen and Stanley Dance.
125.q: No, I don't think so, in fact I think they've mellowed them. And I want to thank you, and Stanley Dance, your very fine husband, for arranging this for me. And I want to tell you how much I really appreciate it, and I hope that I'll be able to justify all of your interests by producing some more…
